title: Smallest Incident Window
summary: Find the shortest stretch of a log that contains every error code involved in an incident.

stages.title: Shortest covering window
stages.requirement:
`log` is a list of event codes in time order. An incident involves the codes in `codes`,
which may contain duplicates: `["E1", "E1"]` means `"E1"` must appear **twice**. Write
`smallest_window(log, codes)` returning the inclusive index range `(start, end)` of the
shortest contiguous window containing every required code (with multiplicity), or `None`.
On ties, return the window that starts **earliest**. If `codes` is empty, return `None`.

```python
log = ["OK", "E2", "E1", "OK", "E3", "E1", "E2", "OK"]
smallest_window(log, ["E1", "E2", "E3"])  # -> (4, 6)
```

Up to 200,000 log entries.

visibleTests.name: test_missing_code
visibleTests.code:
def test_missing_code():
    assert smallest_window(["A", "B"], ["C"]) is None

hiddenTests.name: test_empty_inputs
test_large
hiddenTests.description: Checking every start position against every end is quadratic.
hiddenTests.code:
def test_large():
    log = ["noise"] * 200_000
    log[150_000] = "A"
    log[150_010] = "B"
    log[10] = "A"
    log[199_999] = "B"
    assert smallest_window(log, ["A", "B"]) == (150_000, 150_010)

hints: Expand a right pointer until the window covers every code, then shrink from the left while it still covers.
Track `need[code]` counts and how many requirements are currently satisfied, so 'is the window complete?' is O(1).
Record a window only when it is strictly shorter than the best so far. That keeps the earliest start on ties.

solution.explanation:
This is the classic minimum window substring. `missing` counts outstanding required
occurrences, so window completeness is O(1). The right pointer grows the window, and
once it's complete the left pointer shrinks it while recording candidates. Requiring a
*strictly* shorter window keeps the earliest start on ties. Each index enters and
leaves the window once.
